newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Creditanstalt gain not seen helping sell-off.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Creditanstalt gain not seen helping sell-off.

text.p: A ten percent gain in nine-month operating profit at Creditanstalt was unlikely to improve the chances of a quick sale of Austria's longest running privatisation candidate, analysts said on Thursday.

"The figures came as no great surprise," said Matthew Czepliewicz, banking analyst at Salomon Brothers in London. "Let's put a positive spin on it -- the figures don't make the bank any more unattractive to potential buyers."
Creditanstalt earlier on Thursday said operating profit was up 9.8 percent at 4.65 billion schillings ($430 million), helped by a booming performance of its foreign units.
Creditanstalt's shares were down slightly on the result, but its common stock later moved into positive territory in an overall limp Vienna market.

"The figures were at most slightly better than the market expected," said a trader, adding turnover remained subdued amid a lack of customer interest. "Right now, earnings just don't have much effect on the market," he said.
The Austrian government on Monday asked for new bids for its 70 percent voting stake in the Austrian flagship bank by mid-November.

It reiterated its intention to finalise the deal before year-end, much to the relief of the bank's executives who have long complained about the bad effects of the seemingly endless privatisation debate on the bank's image.
But analysts remain sceptical that the sale can indeed be wrapped up before the Christmas holiday period, barely two months away. "Absolutely no chance," said Czepliewicz.

A further delay in the sale would come as little surprise to observers of what is the country's longest-running sell-off saga in post-war history. They have seen a host of suitors come and go since the bank first was first put up for sale in 1991.

The stop-start privatisation of Austria's most traditional bank has repeatedly faltered on political lobbying for an "Austrian solution" and sometimes open resistance from Creditanstalt's management, strongly allied with the country's conservative political fold.
Last year, Germany's Allianz dropped its interest in the bank amid accusations that it was denied valuable information in the due-diligence process.
CS Holding also left in disillusionment, accusing Austria's political elite of a bias against foreigners.

Finance Minister Viktor Klima has promised to improve the auction process this time around. "There will be an agreement between the finance ministry and Creditanstalt to ensure interested parties have the right to see all relevant information," he said last week.

The most recent offer, from an Austrian-Italian-German consortium grouped around insurer EA-Generali failed last month because of the consortium's reluctance to take on all of the government's 19.9 million shares in the bank.

Sources close to the group said the consortium was likely to rearrange its bid and submit a revamped offer by the government's new deadline, but no official confirmation of those reports was available..

Savings bank Die Erste, which stormed out of the consortium after a last-minute row over its proposal to effectively take control of Creditanstalt by merging the much bigger bank with its own operations, was also believed to be eager to get back in the race, possibly with a new partner.
A valuation by J.P. Morgan last year put the government stake's value at around 18 billion schillings, far above the 14 billion the package would yield at current market prices. ($1=10.72 Schilling)
